MA.7.0124 — Random Sampling

Comparing a Part to the Whole

Objective: Describe random sampling as a method that tends to produce representative samples and support valid inferences.

Prerequisite skill reviewed: Compare a part of a group to the whole group using a ratio or proportion.

Comparing a Part to the Whole

Before learning why random sampling tends to produce representative samples, review how to compare a part of a group to the whole group using a ratio or proportion.

Worked example: 18 of 30 marbles in a jar are blue, so the ratio of blue marbles to all marbles is 18 out of 30.

Brief Review
A ratio compares a part of a group to the whole group. To find the ratio, compare the number of items with a certain characteristic to the total number of items in the group. A ratio can be written as a fraction and, if needed, converted to a percent.
Review Practice

Decide whether each statement about the ratio is correct. Select True or False for each statement.

1) A jar has 40 buttons: 24 silver and 16 gold. The ratio of silver buttons to all buttons is 24 out of 40.
2) In the same jar, the ratio of silver buttons to all buttons is 16 out of 40.
3) 24 out of 40 is equivalent to 60 out of 100, so 60% of the buttons are silver.
Attempts remaining: 3
You have reviewed how to compare a part of a group to the whole group using a ratio. Next, you will explore how random sampling tends to produce samples whose proportions reflect the population, and why this supports valid inferences.

MA.7.0125 — Random Sampling

Solving a Proportion

Objective: Use data from a random sample to draw inferences about a population with an unknown characteristic of interest.

Prerequisite skill reviewed: Solve a proportion to estimate an unknown quantity from a known ratio.

Solving a Proportion

Before using a random sample to estimate an unknown characteristic of a population, review how to solve a proportion to estimate an unknown quantity from a known ratio.

Worked example: 8 out of 20 sampled shoppers prefer Brand X, which is 40% of the sample. Scaling this ratio up estimates about 200 of 500 shoppers would prefer Brand X.

Brief Review
A proportion sets two ratios equal to each other. If you know a ratio from a smaller group, you can use a proportion to estimate the matching quantity in a larger group: set the known ratio equal to an unknown ratio with the same relationship, then solve for the unknown value.
Review Practice

Use the sample ratio to estimate the unknown quantity. Select the correct answer(s) from the list(s).

In a sample of 25 students, 15 prefer online classes, which is % of the sample. Based on this ratio, about students out of 600 would be expected to prefer online classes.
Attempts remaining: 3
You have reviewed how to solve a proportion to estimate an unknown quantity from a known ratio. Next, you will use data from a random sample to draw inferences about a population with an unknown characteristic of interest.
[Existing MA.7.0125 Explain instruction continues here — no changes]
MA.7.0127 — Comparing Data Distributions

Comparing Ranges on a Number Line

Objective: Informally assess the degree of visual overlap of two numerical data distributions with similar variabilities.

Prerequisite skill reviewed: Compare two sets of values plotted on the same number line to determine whether their ranges overlap, and by how much.

Comparing Ranges on a Number Line

Before assessing how much two data distributions overlap, review how to compare two sets of values plotted on the same number line to determine whether their ranges overlap.

Worked example: Interval A spans 3 to 9, and Interval B spans 6 to 12. The intervals overlap between 6 and 9.

Expandable / Collapsible Review
Identify the least and greatest values of each interval. This tells you where each interval begins and ends on the number line.
Look for values that fall within both intervals. These shared values are where the intervals overlap.
Use the shared values to describe where the intervals overlap and how wide that overlapping section is.
Worked Example
Worked Example — Compare Interval A and Interval B above
Step 1 — Find Each Span: Interval A runs from 3 to 9. Interval B runs from 6 to 12.
Step 2 — Find the Shared Values: Both intervals include the values from 6 to 9.
Step 3 — Describe the Overlap: Interval A and Interval B overlap from 6 to 9, a width of 3 units.

MA.7.0129 — Measures of Center

Finding and Describing a Difference

Objective: Use measures of center for numerical data from random samples to draw informal comparative inferences about two populations.

Prerequisite skill reviewed: Find the difference between two numbers and describe what that difference means in context.

Finding and Describing a Difference

Before comparing measures of center between two populations, review how to find the difference between two numbers and describe what that difference means in context.

Worked example: Group A's average score is 74 points and Group B's average score is 81 points, a difference of 7 points.

Brief Review
To compare two numbers, subtract the smaller number from the larger number to find how much greater one is than the other. Then describe the difference using the units and context of the situation.
Worked Example
Worked Example — Group A average score: 74 points. Group B average score: 81 points.
81 − 74 = 7.
Group B's average score is 7 points higher than Group A's average score.
Review Practice

Complete the comparison of the two numbers. Select the correct answer(s) from the list(s).

Bookshelf A holds 18 books. Bookshelf B holds 22 books. Bookshelf B holds books than Bookshelf A.
Attempts remaining: 3
You have reviewed how to find and describe the difference between two numbers. Next, you will use measures of center from random samples to draw informal comparative inferences about two populations.
[Existing MA.7.0129 Explain instruction continues here — no changes]
MA.7.0130 — Measures of Variation

Comparing Two Values

Objective: Use measures of variability for numerical data from random samples to draw informal comparative inferences about two populations.

Prerequisite skill reviewed: Find the difference between two numbers and interpret which value is larger and by how much, in context.

Comparing Two Values

Before comparing measures of variability between two populations, review how to find the difference between two numbers and interpret what a larger or smaller value means in context.

Worked example: Trail A is 5 miles long and Trail B is 9 miles long, a difference of 4 miles.

Brief Review
When comparing two numbers, first find the difference by subtracting the smaller value from the larger value. Then interpret what the size of the difference — and which value is greater — tells you about the situation.
Worked Reminder
Worked Reminder
9 − 5 = 4. Trail B is 4 miles longer than Trail A, so hiking Trail B would likely take more time and effort.
Review Practice

Compare the two values. Select True or False for each statement.

Park A covers 12 acres.
Park B covers 20 acres.
1) Park B is 8 acres larger than Park A.
2) Park A is 8 acres larger than Park B.
3) The difference between the parks' areas is 8 acres.
Attempts remaining: 3
You have reviewed how to compare two values and interpret their difference in context. Next, you will use measures of variability from random samples to draw informal comparative inferences about two populations.
